courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Values in Spatial Planning
courses.description: This course aims to engage students to reflect on value issues in the planning process. It explores competing understandings of how planning should be conducted, what goals planning should achieve, and why planning should be practised in particular ways. It encourages students to examine the value implications of various planning theories for government, the market and civil society, and to develop and justify their own value positions in the planning process.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing this courses, students are expected to be able to:

* Recognise planning as a value-laden practice.
* Identify different values of and in planning.
* Reflect on the role of values in shapping planning decisions and outcomes.
* Develop, articulate and justify personal value positions in planning.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. The values of and in planning
2. Planners’ roles in planning
3. Planning as practice of knowing
4. Planning for public interest
5. Planning for growth
6. Planning beyond growth
7. Planning and informality
8. Planning for multiculturalism
9. Planning and heritage
10. Planning for equal opportunities
11. Planning for the more-than-human
12. Planning in the public and private sectors
13. Planning ethics
courses.feedback_evaluation:

* Qualitative feedback from students inside and outside the classroom throughout the term.

* Reflections of the instructor throughout the term.
* Periodic curriculum review.

For students:

* Verbal feedback during class participation.
* Verbal and written feedback for assessments.

courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Urban AI
courses.description: This course introduces the emerging field of Urban Artificial Intelligence (Urban AI) and its applications in sustainable urban planning. Students will learn fundamental programming skills in Python, key machine learning techniques, and AI-driven methods for analysing spatial, social media, and street view image data. The course integrates theory and practice—covering smart city concepts, big data analytics, and human–AI interactions—to equip students with the analytical and critical thinking skills needed to address complex urban challenges. Through individual essays and group projects, students will apply AI tools to real-world planning and policy issues.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to:

* Explain the theoretical foundations of smart cities and big data, and evaluate their implications for digital governance, planning innovation, and urban sustainability.

* Develop basic programming skills in Python, including data processing, spatial analysis, and visualisation techniques for urban datasets.

* Understand key machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) methods and their relevance to urban research and planning practice.

* Examine human–AI and human–agent interactions in the context of urban systems, exploring trust, usability, and decision-support roles of AI in planning processes.
* Critically evaluate the ethical, social, and governance implications of AI applications in cities, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and responsible innovation.
courses.course_syllabus:
Module 1: Smart Cities, Big Data, and Ethical Urban AI

Lecture 1: Introduction to Smart Cities — theoretical foundations, urban intelligence, and digital transformation in planning.

Lecture 2: AI for urban planning — the rise of AI.

Lecture 3: Urban Sensing and Spatial Data for Urban Planning — geospatial data, GIS integration, and spatial thinking for planners.

Lecture 4: Ethical Considerations and Critiques — data privacy, algorithmic bias, governance, and critical perspectives on smart urbanism.

Module 2: Programming, Machine Learning, and Human–Agent Interaction

Lecture 5: Python Programming Basics I — data structures, control flow, and essential libraries (NumPy, pandas).

Lecture 6: Python Programming Basics II — data visualisation, simple spatial data handling, and automation.

Lecture 7: Machine Learning and AI I — supervised learning and neural networks.

Lecture 8: Machine Learning and AI II — unsupervised learning, clustering, and geospatial prediction models.

Lecture 9: Human–Agent Interaction — Trust, Design, and Collaboration in Urban Planning.

Module 3: Big Data Applications and Emerging Urban AI Tools

Lecture 10: Social Media Analytics — extracting urban insights from social media data; sentiment, mobility, and perception analysis.

Lecture 11: Big Data Applications in Urban Planning — street-view image analysis, the built environment, and AI-driven design evaluation.

Lecture 12: Large Language Models for Urban and Transport Planning — leveraging LLMs for text mining and policy recommendations.
courses.feedback_evaluation:
* Oral feedback will be given after in-class presentations to guide improvement.

* Formative feedback will be provided during lab sessions and consultations on coding, data analysis, and project design.
* Written comments and evaluation will be based on an individual essay and a group project.

courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Smart Sustainable Planning for Human Flourishing
courses.description: This course introduces students to the concept and practice of smart cities. Students are encouraged to explore with different stakeholders to understand what smart initiatives and processes are essential for the well-being of planet, place and people.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, the students will develop the following capacities:

* Comparing and contrasting the diversified and intertwined concepts surrounding smart sustainable cities, and human flourishing
* Evaluating a city through a synthesised understanding of smart sustainability and human flourishing
* Creating solutions that are smart and sustainable, conducive to human flourishing

courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Socio-economic and Environmental Valuation
courses.description: This course aims to introduce valuation techniques that go beyond traditional cost-benefit analysis to enhance students’ capability to assess social and environmental values in the development and planning process. These include social value impact assessment and ecosystem service value assessment.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students will:

• Understand the concepts of sustainability and valuation and their importance.

• Appreciate and apply concepts and methods of valuing ecosystem services.

• Explore theories and methodologies in valuing social impacts.

• Synthesize sustainability valuation to inform decision-making in the planning and development processes.

• Develop a capacity to compare and contrast different valuation methods and generate new approaches to sustainability valuation.

courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Sustainable Planning Laboratory
courses.description: This Laboratory provides a platform for students to explore planning concepts and practices that promote ecological, human-centric, smart, green and resilient urbanism in a concrete context. Using a combination of case study-based lectures and interactive tutorials, students develop a speculative and research-based spatial planning concept which integrates various urban systems. By referring to international and regional cases of innovative planning, students explore how land-use planning, road networks and transport nodes, and urban green networks shape environmental, economic and social sustainability.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.course_syllabus:
The lecture topics for this course are organised according to four different general themes – each theme will be explored through two case study-based lectures by the course instructor or invited experts from academia or planning practice. The themes are:

1. Historic perspectives on integrated sustainable urban planning.

* The Town Planning and New Town Planning movements, 1900 – 2000.
* Top-down versus bottom-up urbanism: Jane Jacobs versus Robert Moses.

2. Recent approaches on sustainable urban development.

* Transport-Oriented Development models and their impact.
* The 15-minute city and other liveable city planning visions.

3. Ecological systems in urban and regional contexts.

* Urban regions, resource supply networks, and sustainability.
* Urban and regional ecologies, biodiversity and climate change.

4. From Macro- to Meso-scale: urban planning, urban design and placemaking.

* Urban massing, green corridors and micro-climates.
* The social value of public spaces.

All lectures will feature spatial planning diagrams and other spatial and visual materials which together provide a catalogue of planning models and environmental design examples suitable for adaptation in student projects. Relevant planning data and social impact dimensions will be discussed to stimulate critical thinking and nuanced, multi-disciplinary design thinking and project evaluation.

Informed by the lectures, students will work in groups of two or three to develop a speculative and research-based spatial planning concept which integrates various urban systems. The planning concept will be developed iteratively through interactive tutorials with the course instructor and through ‘flipped classroom’ peer-review discussions and learning, starting with conceptual abstract city planning models and finishing with a site-specific planning proposal which includes the following urban systems:

1. Land-use planning and density planning.
2. Road networks and transport nodes.
3. Urban green networks.
4. Typical public spaces.

The conceptual plans need to be explored through innovative and integrated approaches, learning from historic, recent and future planning proposals in international, regional and local contexts. Proposals will be evaluated for their demonstrated ability to discuss critical conflicts and opportunities between various development priorities, and how urban planning at macro and meso-scales affect environmental, economic and social sustainability.

The student projects will be documented in an A3 landscape formatting logbook containing lecture notes, case study analysis, planning design sketches and self-evaluation, research-based project development, and final project drawings at macro- and meso-scale.

Projects will be assessed based on a final presentation using a 15-minute PowerPoint and verbal presentation in which all team members present and indicate their individual contributions to the group project. The quality of the PPT and verbal presentation will be assessed, as well as the quality of the project report – requiring a well-documented, comprehensive research narrative in a professional layout with self-explanatory texts and figures. Supporting research should be cited - relevant literature and other external sources should be referenced using APA format and external image materials may be included if sources are properly credited. AI tools may be used for data collection and processing; the use of generative AI tools for producing any project materials, including drawings, diagrams and text descriptions, is not permitted. Students should present projects in their own words to demonstrate learning outcomes.
courses.feedback_evaluation: Students will make weekly submissions of in-progress project documentation. Course instructors will provide verbal feedback during interactive tutorials, focusing on how well the submitted materials incorporate the learning outcomes. Each group will make one combined document submission, each page should indicate individual authors. Final project submissions and presentations are graded according to the grade descriptor criteria.

courses.subject: SDUP
courses.title: Sustainable Urban Planning Thesis
courses.description: This course is the capstone of the Master of Science in Sustainable Urban Planning programme. Each student is required to undertake an independent research thesis under the supervision of an academic advisor. The thesis should demonstrate the student’s ability to integrate planning theories, research methods, and professional knowledge to address real-world urban challenges. Through this process, students develop analytical, critical, and reflective skills essential for professional practice and research in sustainable urban planning.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Sustainable Urban Planning
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to:

* Demonstrate mastery of urban planning theory, methods and practice in the context of sustainability.

* Develop a fully independent research thesis addressing a real-world planning challenge and applying appropriate professional methods.

* Translate research findings into actionable planning policy or design recommendations with clear relevance to professional practice.

* Present a polished, well-structured thesis output that meets the standards of professional communication, ethics and project management.
courses.course_syllabus:
* Library and research methodology workshops to support data collection and analysis.

* Research seminars organised by the SUP to advance the knowledge in urban planning.

* Regular group meetings organised by individual supervisors (e.g. progress review, interim and final presentations).

* Individual consultation meetings between supervisors and students to provide tailored academic guidance and feedback.
courses.feedback_evaluation:
* Supervisors will provide formative feedback during regular meetings.
* Comments will be given on proposal outlines and progress reports to guide improvement.
* Feedback will be provided following the presentation.
* Summative evaluation will be based on the written thesis.
courses.required_readings:
Rudestam, K. E., & Newton, R. R. (2015). *Surviving Your Dissertation: A Comprehensive Guide to Content and Process* (4th ed.). Sage Publications.

Hoover, K. R., & Donovan, T. (2011). *The Elements of Social Scientific Thinking* (10th ed.). Wadsworth.

Creswell, J. W. (2014). *Research Design: Qualitative, Quantitative, and Mixed Methods Approaches* (4th ed.). Sage Publications.
courses.recommended_readings: Morgan, G. (1983). *Beyond Method: Strategies for Social Research*. Sage Publications.
